summary: This Wikipedia article explains post-glacial rebound (isostatic rebound), the slow rise of land after the weight of last-glacial ice sheets was removed, and the viscoelastic mantle flow that accompanies it. It covers effects on vertical and horizontal crustal motion, global sea level, tilt of lakes, gravity, vertical datums, intraplate earthquakes and volcanism, and its relevance to monitoring recent global warming. It also covers applications to mantle viscosity and ice history, the history of discovery in Sweden, Finnish property law, and the sea-level equation.
one_line: Wikipedia article on post-glacial rebound, the ongoing rise of land after the removal of ice sheets, and its wide geophysical effects.
key_facts: Post-glacial rebound is also called isostatic rebound or crustal rebound and is the rise of land masses after removal of the weight of ice sheets during the last glacial period.
Ice sheets during the last glacial period reached up to three kilometres thick at the glacial maximum about 20,000 years ago.
Typical present-day uplift rates are of the order of 1 cm/year or less.
Studies suggest that post-glacial rebound will continue for at least another 10,000 years.
In Finland, the total area of the country is growing by about seven square kilometers per year.
The peak GPS-measured uplift rate in the north part of the Gulf of Bothnia is about 11 mm/year.
Global sea level fell by about 120 metres at the last glacial maximum, exposing continental shelves.
The Gulf of Bothnia is predicted to eventually close up at Kvarken in more than 2,000 years; Kvarken is a UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site.
Lake Mälaren in Sweden became a freshwater lake in about the 12th century when uplift cut it off from the Baltic Sea, at the time Stockholm was founded at its outlet.
In Great Britain, northern Scotland rises up to 10 cm per century while southern England sinks up to 5 cm per century.
The magnitude 8 New Madrid earthquake of 1811 in mid-continental US is cited as an important intraplate earthquake.
Glacial loads provided more than 30 MPa of vertical stress in northern Canada and more than 20 MPa in northern Europe during glacial maximum.
Rebound stress available to trigger earthquakes today is of the order of 1 MPa, enough to reactivate pre-existing faults close to failure.
Decreasing pressure due to deglaciation can increase melt production and volcanic activity below Iceland and Greenland by 20-30 times.
Unusually rapid present rebound of up to 4.1 cm/year in the Amundsen Sea embayment of Antarctica is predicted to provide a modest stabilizing influence on West Antarctic marine ice sheet instability.

Anders Celsius initiated rock marks along the Swedish coast; by 1765 it was concluded that the sea-level change was an uneven rise of land, and Gerard De Geer's 1890 work on old shorelines led to acceptance of the theory.
